Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ be bounded. Then $ST$ and $TS$ are trace class and $$\operatorname{tr}(ST)=\operatorname{tr}(TS) .$$ If $A,B\in\mathcal B(H)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), then the products $AB$ and $BA$ are trace class and $$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a normed space, let $D \subseteq X$ be a dense normed subspace, let $Y$ be a Banach space, and let $T:D\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator. Then there is a unique bounded linear operator $\widetilde T:X\to Y$ such that $$\widetilde T|_D = T,$$ and $\|\widetilde T\| = \|T\|$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if $$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$ for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**. Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The **operator norm** of $T$ is $$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$ The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]). In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice principle is used for this assertion. The same number is the least bound of $T$: $$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$ If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives $$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$ When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$, so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a real constant $C \ge 0$ such that $$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$ Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

derivations.claim: [The parenthesisation isometry] The map $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$ is multilinear from $H^n$ into $H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)}$, so by [F2] applied to the two parenthesisations of the $n$-fold algebraic tensor product it defines a linear map on the algebraic tensor product, and this linear map preserves inner products on elementary tensors by [F1]: $\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle=\prod_k\langle v_k,w_k\rangle=\langle v_1,w_1\rangle\langle v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_2\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle$. Since the elementary tensors span a dense subspace and both sides are complete, [F8] and this isometry identity give a linear isometry $J_n$ on the completed tensor powers, and the image is closed and contains all elementary tensors $v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$, whose span is dense by [F1]; hence $J_n$ is surjective. This proves (b). [F1, F2, F8, algebra]

[The first-slot operator] By [F3] the operator $O\otimes I_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}\in\mathcal B(H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)})$ is bounded with $(O\otimes I)(u\otimes w)=Ou\otimes w$. Transporting it through the isometry $J_n$ of clause (b) gives a bounded operator $A_1:=J_n^{-1}(O\otimes I)J_n$ on $H^{\otimes n}$ with $A_1(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=J_n^{-1}(Ov_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n))=Ov_1\otimes v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ for all $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$. [F1, F3, algebra]

[The zero extension and its symmetry] Regard $\rho$ as an endomorphism of $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and put $\widetilde\rho:=P_\sigma^{(n)}\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$, an endomorphism of $H^{\otimes n}$ whose restriction to $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ is $\rho$ and which vanishes on the orthogonal complement; then $\widetilde\rho\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\widetilde\rho=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ by [F6] and [F7], so $\widetilde\rho$ is a density operator on $H^{\otimes n}$ with $\widetilde\rho=P_\sigma^{(n)}\widetilde\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$. Since $U_\pi$ preserves $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and acts on it as the scalar $\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)$ by [F4], $U_\pi\widetilde\rho U_\pi^*=\widetilde\rho$ for every $\pi$. [F4, F6, F7, algebra]

[Slot operators and the permutation invariance of their sum] Fix $i$, choose $\pi\in S_n$ with $\pi(1)=i$ and set $O^{(i)}:=U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$; [F9] and step 1.2 give $\|O^{(i)}\|=\|O\otimes I\|\le\|O\|$, and [F3], [F4] give $(O^{(i)})^*=U_\pi(O^*\otimes I)U_\pi^*=(O^*)^{(i)}$, so $O=O^*$ gives $O^{(i)}=(O^{(i)})^*$. On elementary tensors, [F4] gives $U_\pi^*(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi(n)}$; step 1.2 replaces the first factor by $Ov_{\pi(1)}=Ov_i$; and $U_\pi$ then moves that factor to slot $\pi(1)=i$, leaving every other factor in its original slot, so $O^{(i)}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Ov_i\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$. If $\pi'$ is another permutation with $\pi'(1)=i$, then $\tau:=\pi^{-1}\pi'$ fixes $1$ and $U_\tau A_1U_\tau^*$ agrees with $A_1$ on elementary tensors by [F1], [F3], hence equals it by [F8]; thus $U_{\pi'}A_1U_{\pi'}^*=U_\pi U_\tau A_1U_\tau^*U_\pi^*=U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*$ and $O^{(i)}$ is well defined, with the displayed elementary-tensor action. For $\tau\in S_n$ one then has $U_\tau O^{(i)}U_\tau^*=U_{\tau\pi}A_1U_{\tau\pi}^*=O^{(\tau(i))}$, and summing over $i$ with $\tau$ permuting $\{1,\dots,n\}$ gives $U_\tau\Sigma(O)U_\tau^*=\Sigma(O)$ for $\Sigma(O):=\sum_{i=1}^nO^{(i)}$; equivalently $\Sigma(O)$ commutes with every $U_\tau$. Since $P_\sigma^{(n)}=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)U_\pi$ is a finite linear combination of the $U_\pi$ by [F4], $\Sigma(O)$ commutes with $P_\sigma^{(n)}$, so it preserves $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and its orthogonal complement and $\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)}=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)}$; this proves (a) and (c). [F1, F3, F4, F8, F9, step 1.2, algebra]

[Reduction to one slot, the trace law and the reduced operator] Fix $i$ and $\pi$ with $\pi(1)=i$; by steps 1.3 and 2.1 and [F7], $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho O^{(i)})=\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*)=\operatorname{tr}(U_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi A_1)=\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)$, where the middle equality is cyclicity and the last uses $U_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi=\widetilde\rho$. Therefore $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\,\Sigma(O))=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho O^{(i)})=n\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)=n\operatorname{tr}((O\otimes I)J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1})=n\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1})O)$ by [F7], [F5] and the explicit form of $A_1$ in step 1.2; with the definition of $\gamma$ this is (d). By [F5] clause (b) applied with $R=J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1}$, which is positive of trace one by step 1.3, the operator $\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1}$ is positive of trace one, so its conjugate $\gamma$ is a density operator on $H$. If instead another named slot is retained, the same computation with the corresponding slot operator produces $\gamma'$ with $n\operatorname{tr}((\gamma'-\gamma)O)=0$ for every $O\in\mathcal B(H)$, hence $\gamma'=\gamma$ on testing against the rank-one operators $O=T_{u,v}$, for which $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma T_{u,v})=\langle\gamma u,v\rangle$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]); this proves (e) as well. [F5, F7, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

[Conclusion and scope] Step 1.1 proves (b), step 2.1 proves (a) and (c), and step 3.1 proves (d) and (e); every argument used only the finite-dimensional tensor construction, the permutation sectors, the partial trace and the trace axioms, and no physical object, preparation or measurement entered, which is clause (f). [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and $$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
For all real $x,y$, $$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection. Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$, $$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$ Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: [Exponential comparison] Since $\beta\varepsilon>0$, strict increase in [F3] gives $\exp(\beta\varepsilon)>\exp(0)=1$, and [F3] gives $\exp(-\beta\varepsilon)=1/\exp(\beta\varepsilon)\in(0,1)$; consequently $1<Z=1+\exp(-\beta\varepsilon)<2$. [F3, algebra]

[The canonical operator] By [F1] with $E_0=0$, $E_1=\varepsilon$ and $(v_1,v_2)=(u_0,u_1)$, $Z=1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$ and $\rho_\beta=Z^{-1}(T_{u_0,u_0}+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}T_{u_1,u_1})\in\mathcal D$, so $\rho_\beta$ is a density operator; its two weights are $Z^{-1}$ and $e^{-\beta\varepsilon}Z^{-1}$, which are distinct because $\exp(-\beta\varepsilon)\ne1$ by step 1.1. [Reduced preparation of product-type states] Let $u_1,\dots,u_N$ be pairwise orthonormal, put $x:=u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_N$ and let $\Psi$ be the unit vector of clause (c) for $\sigma=-$ or $\sigma=+$; both satisfy $P_\sigma^{(N)}\Psi=\Psi$ by [F4], and both equal $\sqrt{N!}\,P_\sigma^{(N)}x$. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]

derivations.claim: [Entropy conservation] Let $\rho(0)=\sum_iw_iT_{u_i,u_i}$ be the spectral decomposition of [F2]. By [F1], $U(t)$ is unitary, so $(U(t)u_i)$ is an orthonormal basis and $\rho(t)=\sum_iw_iT_{U(t)u_i,U(t)u_i}$: the eigenvalues of $\rho(t)$ are the same $w_i$ with the same multiplicities. By [F2] the entropy depends only on that multiset, so $s(\rho(t))=s(\rho(0))$ for every $t$. This proves (a). [F1, F2, algebra]

[Stationarity of the canonical preparation] By [F3] $\rho_\beta$ is diagonal in the eigenbasis $(v_j)$ of $H_N^\sigma$; the same basis diagonalizes $U(t)$ with eigenvalues $e^{-itE_j/\hbar}$, so $U(t)T_{v_j,v_j}U(t)^*=T_{v_j,v_j}$ for every $j$ and hence $U(t)\rho_\beta U(t)^*=\rho_\beta$. Every thermal mean $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta A)$ is therefore time independent by [F1]. This proves (b). [F1, F3, algebra]

[No unitary production of the canonical preparation] Suppose $\rho(t)=\rho_\beta$ for some $t$. Applying the unitary $U(t)^*$ on both sides and using $U(t)^*=U(t)^{-1}$ from [F1], $\rho(0)=U(t)^*\rho_\beta U(t)=\rho_\beta$ by step 1.2 applied to $-t$. Hence $\rho(0)\ne\rho_\beta$ implies $\rho(t)\ne\rho_\beta$ for every $t$, which is (c). [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

[Conclusion and scope] Steps 1.1-2.1 prove (a)-(c). The argument used only the unitary flow, the eigenvalue multiset of a preparation and the spectral form of $\rho_\beta$; no environment, measurement model, readout equilibration or laboratory sample entered, which is (d). [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

derivations.claim: [Diagonalisation] In the basis $(|1\rangle,|2\rangle)$ the operator $h$ has the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-t\\-t&0\end{pmatrix}$; the vectors $u_\mp=(|1\rangle\mp|2\rangle)/\sqrt2$ are orthogonal unit vectors and $h u_\mp=\mp t\,u_\mp$ by direct evaluation, so $\{u_-,u_+\}$ is an orthonormal eigenbasis with eigenvalues $-t$ and $t$ by [[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]. Hence $h+t\,\mathrm{id}$ has the eigenvalues $0$ on $u_-$ and $2t$ on $u_+$, and it satisfies the hypothesis of [L1] with $\varepsilon=2t$, $u_0=u_-$, $u_1=u_+$. This proves (a). [L1, algebra]

[Canonical data] Applying [L1] with $\varepsilon=2t$ gives $Z=1+e^{-2\beta t}$ and $\rho_\beta=Z^{-1}(T_{u_-,u_-}+e^{-2\beta t}T_{u_+,u_+})$ for $h+t\,\mathrm{id}$; since $h=(h+t\,\mathrm{id})-t\,\mathrm{id}$ and both operators are functions of the same eigenbasis, the Gibbs operator of $h$ is the same $\rho_\beta$, because the Gibbs weights are unchanged by the shift of all levels by the constant $t$ (the explicit weights depend only on the differences of the levels). The mean of $h+t\,\mathrm{id}$ is $2t/(e^{2\beta t}+1)\in(0,t)$, so $\langle h\rangle_\beta=2t/(e^{2\beta t}+1)-t=-t\tanh(\beta t)$, which lies in $(-t,0)$ because $e^{2\beta t}>1$ for $\beta t>0$; the entropy formula is that of [L1] at $\varepsilon=2t$ and satisfies $0\le s<\log2$ by [L1], and $F=-\beta^{-1}\log(1+e^{-2\beta t})-t$ is the free energy of $h$ by [L2] and [L1]. This proves (b) and (c) apart from the scope clause. [L1, L2, step 1.1, algebra]

derivations.claim: [Dilute identities] With $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}\in(0,1)$ the bosonic mean of [L1] is $1/(e^{\beta\varepsilon}-1)=q/(1-q)$ and the fermionic mean is $1/(e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1)=q/(1+q)$; the algebraic identities $q/(1-q)=q+q^2/(1-q)$ and $q/(1+q)=q-q^2/(1+q)$ are exact for every $q\in(0,1)$, and the remainders $q^2/(1-q)$, $q^2/(1+q)$ are positive. This proves (a). [L1, algebra]

[The finite check at $q=1/10$] At $q=1/10$ the bosonic mean is $(1/10)/(9/10)=1/9$ and the fermionic mean is $(1/10)/(11/10)=1/11$; the remainders are $q^2/(1-q)=(1/100)/(9/10)=1/90$ and $q^2/(1+q)=(1/100)/(11/10)=1/110$, so the exact identities $1/9=1/10+1/90=10/90+1/90$ and $1/11=1/10-1/110=11/110-1/110$ hold. This proves (b). [L1, algebra]

[The two convergence examples] For $\varepsilon_j=j\varepsilon$ the sum is $\sum_{j\ge1}(e^{-\beta\varepsilon})^j=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}/(1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon})<\infty$ by [L2], and for the bosonic product one needs in addition $\mu<\inf_j\varepsilon_j=\varepsilon$; for $\varepsilon_j\equiv\varepsilon$ every term of the sum equals $e^{-\beta\varepsilon}>0$, so the sum diverges and [L2] makes both product partitions infinite. This proves (c). [L2, algebra]

[Checks and scope] Steps 1.1-1.3 give the exact identities, the exact rational check, and the two convergence outcomes; every quantity is computed in the declared mode models at the assigned temperature, and no measured occupation, dilute gas, thermodynamic limit or condensation entered, which is (d). [L1, L2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎
